## Purpose

This is a decision-facing proposal, distinct from the reproducible
statistical analysis in `notebooks/09_sampling_campaign_design.qmd`
(which it cites, not repeats): given roughly one year before thesis
writing, what should a real chloride sampling program at SBRR and SBGG
actually look like, at what cost, and what does each tier of effort
answer?

**Updated direction**: rather than waiting for a conventional spring
field season to start the intensive calibration window, this proposal
now plans to begin it as soon as possible (this fall/winter), since
the conductivity loggers are already running and a delay only wastes
already-accumulating baseline conductance record. The intensive window
should then be followed by roughly monthly chloride sampling for a
full annual cycle -- not just through one field season -- specifically
so the calibration can be tested against winter, spring-runoff,
summer, and fall conditions, rather than extrapolated from a single
season.

## How many calibration pairs (n) are actually needed?

There is no real Cl-EC paired dataset yet to run a formal power analysis
against -- that is exactly the gap this campaign is meant to close, so
any number offered here is a reasoned target, not a computed certainty.
Standard practical guidance for a simple linear calibration regression:

- **n = 15-20** real paired samples is the conventional practical
  minimum for a stable slope/intercept estimate in a simple linear
  regression, assuming the relationship is close to linear across the
  sampled range.
- **n = 30-40** is a more defensible target once seasonal variation is
  considered -- a single season's worth of pairs risks fitting a
  relationship that doesn't generalize to winter/spring conditions (a
  real, stated limitation of the current ~5-week summer-only EC record
  used in `notebooks/09`). A full year of monthly sampling plus the
  intensive window (below) comfortably clears this target without
  relying on one season's data.
- Once a first real regression exists, its own residual variance can be
  used to compute an actual power/precision target for any further
  refinement -- a genuine next step, not possible to pre-compute now.

## Should calibration samples also carry other analytes/isotopes?

**Yes, and the marginal cost is worth it.** Chloride alone cannot
distinguish simple dilution/mixing from evaporative concentration, and
cannot independently confirm that a sample is behaving conservatively.
Two real, complementary additions:

- **Major ions (Na, K, Ca, Mg, SO4, alkalinity)**: the same real
  chemistry this project's own mixing-fraction analysis
  (`notebooks/06`) already uses to test whether a sample's SI/speciation
  is consistent with conservative mixing. Adding these to every
  calibration sample turns each one into a real mixing-model data point,
  not just a Cl-EC pair.
- **Delta-18O/delta-D isotopes**: the one analysis that can distinguish
  evaporative concentration (which would shift isotopes along an
  evaporation trend line) from simple conservative mixing (which would
  not) -- neither Cl nor major ions alone can make this distinction.
  Isotopes cost meaningfully more per sample than major ions and should
  be prioritized for a subset of samples (e.g. the Tier 1 intensive
  window below), not necessarily every single sample.

## Why these intervals: the evidence in brief

The intervals come from a Monte Carlo test on the real SBRR and SBGG conductance record (notebook 09, `notebooks/09_sampling_campaign_design.qmd`): 200 random start days per interval, rebuild by interpolation, error as a percent of the mean, with air-exposed days removed. Reconstruction error is 3 to 5 percent for daily and every-other-day sampling, 7 to 8 percent weekly (worst 10) and 9 to 10 percent biweekly (worst 12 to 13), rising smoothly with no cliff. That supports a short daily window (2 weeks, or 4 weeks if the budget allows) to get matched pairs and the daily cycle, followed by monthly or biweekly sampling for seasonal stability. The same notebook shows the two loggers are close to opposite in phase over the day, so both stations are sampled in a fixed 10:00 to 13:00 window each visit. Notebook 01 gives the temporal structure (diurnal cycle and persistence) behind this and notebook 02 compares conductance with discharge and weather once discharge is complete. These are results on conductance, not chloride; the chloride models have only been run on simulated data. The advisor summary is `docs/outreach/sampling_plan_advisor.qmd`; this document is the full record.

## The proposed design at a glance

The campaign is centered on the two existing conductivity-logger
stations, **SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) and SBGG (Geiger Grade,
downstream)**, and @tbl-samplingplan summarizes what is sampled, how
often, and why. Calibration models (linear, log-linear, and a
generalized additive model [@wood2017], with a random forest [@breiman2001]
as a skill benchmark) are validated with rolling-origin, time-aware
cross-validation [@bergmeir2012] so that autocorrelation does not inflate
apparent skill.

| Site | What is sampled | Frequency / timing | Why |
|------------------|----------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) | Chloride, major ions (Na, K, Ca, Mg, SO4, alkalinity), field pH/temperature/specific conductance | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks (intensive window, starting fall/winter 2026) | Establishes the calibration's short-timescale behavior and noise floor against the logger's continuous record. |
| SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream) | Same analyte set as SBRR | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks, concurrent with SBRR | A second, independently calibrated site tests whether one relationship serves the whole system or each site needs its own equation. |
| SBRR and SBGG | Same analyte set | Monthly for a full annual cycle after the intensive window | Tests seasonal stability across winter baseflow, spring runoff, summer baseflow, and fall transition. |
| SBRR and SBGG (opportunistic) | Same analyte set | Additional samples around large storms and spring snowmelt | These are the conditions most likely to break conservative mixing (dilution, flashy runoff). |
| SBRR and SBGG (subset) | delta-18-O / delta-D isotopes | Roughly one isotope sample per season, with a regular chloride visit | Chloride alone cannot distinguish thermal/meteoric mixing from evaporative concentration; isotopes can. |

: Proposed chloride sampling plan at the two conductivity-logger stations. {#tbl-samplingplan}

## Additional candidate sampling sites

- **The active steaming fissure / capped wellhead** (Lower Sinter
  Terrace, active since June 2025): a novel end-member close to the
  eruption vent itself. The property is not Ormat's and I have access to
  it, so access does not limit sampling here. Benefit: it directly tests
  whether the 2025 event reflects a change in the deep upflow chemistry,
  not just a surface reconfiguration. Cost: the laboratory cost of the
  added samples, plus ordinary field safety around hot ground and steam.
- **SBW_0001/SBW_0002 (the Steamboat Hot Springs "resort" wells)**:
  already real, already-sampled locations in this database (per
  `notebooks/06`'s real mixing-fraction analysis, which already includes
  these). Adding them to the *ongoing* calibration campaign (not just a
  one-time 2026 sample) is low-incremental-cost since they are already
  known, accessible sampling points -- a strong candidate for inclusion
  at essentially every tier below.

uc <- unit_costs(); so <- sampling_options()
lt_cost <- (34 + 4) * uc$sample + 4 * uc$batch + 4 * 35 + 2 * uc$isotope

The prices come from the invoice for the seven samples already analyzed. The administration fee is treated as per batch but is unconfirmed, and shipping ($20 to $50 per shipment) is not on the invoice, so every total below carries a range; isotopes are a $40 planning estimate.

```{r cost-unit-06}

knitr::kable(data.frame(Code = li$code, Item = li$item, `Invoice, 7 samples (USD)` = sprintf("%.2f", li$invoice_usd), Charged = li$scales_with, `Unit cost (USD)` = sprintf("%.2f", li$unit_usd), check.names = FALSE), align = "llrlr", caption = "Invoice for one batch of seven samples and the derived unit costs. The administration fee is assumed to be per batch (to confirm); shipping is not on the invoice.")
```

I propose creek sampling at SBRR and SBGG from December 2026 to September 2027, ending in early fall, after a seven-day daily window in November and with two storm or snowmelt events. Monthly sampling is the minimum that spans winter baseflow, runoff and summer; biweekly sampling doubles the paired dates, with the biweekly samples held and shipped together each month. Each frequency is priced with and without isotopes. Weekly sampling is not proposed because it is not feasible for one person. Every sampling date at both stations also gives a thermal-water discharge estimate (two-station chloride balance, gauge discharge at no laboratory cost).

```{r cost-options-06}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Option = so$option, `Chemistry visits` = so$chem_cadence, `Isotope samples` = so$iso_samples, `Chemistry samples (with QA)` = so$chem_samples, Shipments = so$shipments, check.names = FALSE), align = "llrrr", caption = "Design of the sampling options (7-day daily window, two storm events, 10 percent QA). Option C adds four fissure-area sites monthly with isotopes.")
```

```{r cost-options-cost-06}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Option = so$option, `Central total` = fmt_usd(so$total), Range = paste0(fmt_usd(so$total_low), "-", fmt_usd(so$total_high)), `Discharge estimates` = so$discharge_dates, `Cost per estimate` = fmt_usd(so$cost_per_discharge), check.names = FALSE), align = "lrlrr", caption = "Laboratory cost of the same options. Central: fee per batch, $35 per shipment, monthly shipments. Range: shipping $20 to $50, fee per sample, up to one shipment per visit.")
```

With the Lower Terrace samples (34 analyses, 4 duplicates and blanks, four shipments, 2 isotope samples; about `r fmt_usd(lt_cost)`), the central totals are `r fmt_usd(so$total[2] + lt_cost)` (A2), `r fmt_usd(so$total[4] + lt_cost)` (B2) and `r fmt_usd(so$total[5] + lt_cost)` (C). B2 is the working choice and A1 (`r fmt_usd(so$total[1] + lt_cost)`) the fallback. The administration-fee basis and shipping are unconfirmed, so the totals carry the ranges shown; a written quotation will replace them.

**What the baseline says about detecting change.** The mixing results give each Lower Terrace feature a fingerprint: its chloride, its fraction of fissure water (from chloride, with SBRR as the dilute end), and its Cl/B and Na/Cl ratios. If two single samples are compared and each carries a 5 percent analytical error, a difference below about 14 percent in chloride cannot be told from chance, which is a change of 0.08 to 0.15 in the fissure fraction depending on the feature (the well SBW_0001 is the most sensitive, the fissure and resort tank the least). The ratios are less useful than hoped. Cl/B runs only from 20 to 23 across the features and Na/Cl from 0.77 to 0.85, differences smaller than the roughly 20 percent that two single ratios could differ by chance, so the ratios cannot yet separate the features from one another. They can still show a large change in the source, and they are the check that tells dilution (chloride moves, ratios do not) from a change in the fluid (ratios move) once repeat samples tighten the baseline.

**What a change at the springs or fissure would look like at the creek.** At SBBV, thermal water is about 14 percent of the flow but about 86 percent of the chloride, so a fractional change in the thermal chloride flux shows up in creek chloride almost one for one. With the analytical error and a 9 percent reconstruction error for the biweekly record, a single creek comparison would need a change of about 33 percent in thermal chloride flux to stand out. Averaging the ten or so samples taken in each period lowers that to roughly 10 percent, which is why the repeat sampling matters more than any single round. These are planning numbers from one snapshot and no replicates, not tests, and replicate samples at the first visits will replace the assumed 5 percent.

**Why a fissure-centered tier.** Option C adds four sites near the fissure (the capped pipe and fissure vent, SBW_0001, SBS_0001 and SBW_0002) to the biweekly creek program, sampled monthly with isotopes. The reason is that the creek only integrates the thermal inflow, and the sites above it are where a change in the source would appear first and in a form (ratios, silica, isotopes) that the creek chloride cannot show. A change at the fissure that is followed by a change in creek chloride and in the SBRR to SBBV chloride flux would link the two; a change at the creek with no change at the fissure and springs would point to dilution or to inflow from somewhere else. The figure shows the baseline each of these would be compared against.

```{r detect-06, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
source(file.path(root, "scripts/analysis/change_detection_from_mixing.R"))
local({ con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), file.path(root, "database/geochem_operational.sqlite"), flags = RSQLite::SQLITE_RO); on.exit(DBI::dbDisconnect(con)); invisible(change_detection_from_mixing(con, out_dir = file.path(root, "data/derived/change_detection"), fig_dir = file.path(root, "output/figures/manuscript"))) })
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![Baseline fingerprint of each Lower Terrace feature with the smallest change two single samples could show (5 percent analytical error). Planning values.](%s)", normalizePath(file.path(root, "output/figures/manuscript/change_detection_fingerprint.png"), winslash = "/")))
```

## Station locations: the Steamboat Ditch season and the SBGG logger

Steamboat Ditch joins Steamboat Creek just below SBRR and, by field knowledge still to be confirmed by measurement, supplies much of the flow below that point from about May to September. In that season SBRR is a low-flow reach above the confluence and is not the background water for the thermal reach, so the July to October provisional flux, which used SBRR as the upstream term, is a bound. The 1 May 2026 chloride balance is not affected: the samples were taken shortly before the ditch began to carry water.

The proposed refinement has three parts. When the ditch is on, the upstream station would be a site just below the confluence, where the combined water is already summed, so the balance keeps the form $Q_{TW} = (Q_d C_d - Q_u C_u)/C_{TW}$ with no separate ditch term; when it is off, SBRR remains the upstream station. The downstream logger, SBGG, would move upstream to a point above the Cranes Ditch diversion, because dirt infill in the creek before September 2026 lowered the flow there and the logger began to read open air in late September. And one field day with a hydrologist would measure channel transects at both new sites so discharge can be measured by velocity-area and a stage-discharge relation built where there is no gauge. Ditch discharge and chloride would also be measured just above the confluence at a few early visits. The summer record from the new upstream site is not continuous with the 2026 SBRR record, so the old and new sites should overlap briefly if possible. The dates the ditch carries water and the location of the diversion are to be confirmed in the field. The same text, with the supporting figures, is in the thesis proposal's sampling plan.

### Phase 1 (calibration window) and Phase 2 (monthly or biweekly) priced separately

The campaign has two parts that answer different questions. **Phase 1**, the intensive calibration window (notebook 09, Tier 1), is daily sampling at SBRR and SBGG for 2 to 4 weeks with isotopes every third day; it supplies the first real chloride and conductance pairs and is the only way to test whether chloride follows the diurnal conductance signal. **Phase 2** (Tier 2) is the monthly or biweekly sampling afterwards, which tests seasonal stability. The window length is not settled, so three lengths are priced.

```{r phase-split-06}
ps <- phase_split()
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Window (days)` = ps$window_days, `Phase 2 option` = ps$phase2, `Phase 1 samples` = ps$phase1_samples, `Phase 1 cost` = fmt_usd(ps$phase1_cost), `Phase 2 samples` = ps$phase2_samples, `Phase 2 cost` = fmt_usd(ps$phase2_cost), `Combined` = fmt_usd(ps$combined), check.names = FALSE), align = "rllrrrr", caption = "Phase 1 and Phase 2 laboratory cost, central scenario, creek sites only (Lower Terrace and fissure-area sites extra).")
```

Not in the laboratory cost: every SBGG visit needs a manual discharge measurement because SBGG has no gauge (SBRR is read from USGS gauge 10349300), which is field time and equipment, not a laboratory charge. Without it SBGG can calibrate chloride against conductance but cannot give a flux. The earlier tables in this section used a seven-day window; the 14-day row is closer to the notebook's recommendation.

## Tiered proposal: 20 / 40 / 60+ total lab analyses across the year

| Tier | Total analyses/year | What it buys | What it can't answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **20** | ~20 Cl-only or Cl+major-ion analyses | A bare-minimum first Cl-EC calibration point per site, likely just for the intensive window | No seasonal resolution; can't test whether the calibration holds across a full year; no isotope cross-check |
| **40** | ~40 analyses, Cl+major ions on all, isotopes on a subset | Real seasonal resolution across a full year (intensive fall/winter window + roughly monthly follow-through through the following fall, per `notebooks/09`); a real mixing-model check on every sample | Isotope coverage still partial; fissure/resort sites only lightly sampled |
| **60+** | 60+ analyses, isotopes on most/all, includes SBW_0001/0002 routinely and the fissure site | The most complete real dataset: full-year seasonal Cl-EC calibration, mixing-model validation, isotope-based evaporation/mixing discrimination, and a real fissure/resort-well comparison | Cost and lab-turnaround logistics become the real constraint, not the science |

**Recommendation**: Tier 2 (~40 analyses) is the realistic target for a
one-person thesis field campaign within a year -- it is the smallest
tier that actually closes the calibration-and-seasonality gap this whole
project's Cl-EC-proxy premise depends on, and now explicitly assumes an
earlier (fall/winter, not spring) start to the intensive window so the
full year of monthly follow-through sampling fits inside the proposed
timeline. Tier 3 is worth pursuing (e.g. adding the fissure site,
or if the laboratory budget allows) rather than being a hard
requirement.
